answer.answer:
Delivering a non-repeating timber facade off site rests on four upstream requirements, and not one of them is a machine: precise up-front planning and logistics, design for manufacture and assembly, early contractor involvement, and an integrated supply chain, all of them organisational rather than equipment. The non-repeating part pulls in a second chain: bespoke, one-off design actively constrains modularity, so the route to panel-by-panel variation runs through a highly standardised component set feeding a configurator or kit-of-parts, which is what carries mass-customisation. Watch the regulatory side, since prefabrication also depends on resolving compliance, certification and traceability for factory-made assemblies. On envelope energy performance, the record holds no certification scheme of that kind, so nothing here supports a claim about meeting a named energy standard.

**What prefabrication itself requires**

Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) is drawn on by 20 of the 50 coded cases [1], and four things sit upstream of it:

- Prefabrication/off-site (PR2) dependsOn Rely on precise planning (RI14), because prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics; the edge is carried by 18 of the 50 coded cases [1], and RI14 itself is drawn on by 36 of the 50 coded cases [1]. This is by far the heaviest of the requirements, and it is a Risk, an exposure you carry rather than a capability you buy.
- PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" enablesCapability PR2, since DfMA orients the project toward offsite manufacture; the edge is carried by 15 of the 50 coded cases [1]. PR9 is drawn on by 15 of the 50 coded cases [1].
- CO11 "Early contractor involvement" enablesCapability PR2: integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase, and a delivery method that brings participants into early design should be selected; the edge is carried by 13 of the 50 coded cases [1]. CO11 is drawn on by 14 of the 50 coded cases [1], and it also feeds the integrated design-DFAB process and DfMA itself (DEP65, carried by 10 cases [1]; DEP77, carried by 11 cases [1]).
- VA14 "Integrate supply chain" enablesCapability PR2, supply chain integration supporting the offsite production line; the edge is carried by 12 of the 50 coded cases [1], with VA14 drawn on by 14 of the 50 coded cases [1].

These are not four equal requirements: precise planning is drawn on more than twice as often as any of the others. All four are backed by peer-reviewed evidence.

A fifth dependency is regulatory rather than productive: PR2 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", on the grounds that a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability; the edge is carried by 10 of the 50 coded cases [1], with RI18 drawn on by 12 cases [1]. That is the nearest the record comes to envelope certification, and it is about compliance machinery for factory-made parts, not about an energy performance target.

**Non-repeating panels**

The record treats one-off geometry as a constraint, not a free variable: AT1 "Bespoke/customised design" constrains AT2 "Modular", because integral architecture couples functions tightly to components and so constrains modular interchange; the edge is carried by only 4 of the 50 coded cases [1], and AT1 is drawn on by 10 cases [1] against 12 for AT2 [1].

The productive route to panel variation runs the other way, through standardisation: AT7 "Highly standardised" enablesCapability AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts", on the basis that modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components; the edge is carried by 11 of the 50 coded cases [1] and rests on a standard rather than peer-reviewed evidence. AR6 in turn enablesCapability PR11 "Mass-customisation", a design configurator integrating customisation data into robotic manufacturing; that edge is carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases [1], with peer-reviewed backing. AT7 is drawn on by 25 of the 50 cases [1], AR6 by 12 [1], PR11 by 17 [1]. The cost to watch is on the same axis: RI15 "Design compromise/over standardised" is drawn on by 17 of the 50 coded cases [1]. Standardisation also pays back directly: AT7 enablesCapability VA7 "Reduce construction complexity", the base module standard reducing component variety and coordinating design, manufacture and assembly; carried by 15 of the 50 coded cases [1].

**What the off-site route returns**

PR2 enablesCapability VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency", offsite factory work compressing the schedule, carried by 19 of the 50 cases [1]; PR2 enablesCapability VA3 "Improve quality/performance" through the controlled factory environment, carried by 18 [1]; PR2 enablesCapability VA10 "Reduce errors/constraints", factory-based production improving quality control and reducing rework, carried by 14 [1]; and PR2 enablesCapability VA13 "Improve site safety", moving work offsite improving site safety, carried by 12 [1]. This last is the only cited path to site safety in front of me, though VA13 is drawn on by 39 of the 50 coded cases [1].

If disassembly and material recovery matter for the envelope, two further peer-reviewed links apply, both thin in carriage: VA9 "Allow traceable/linked data" enablesCapability VA15 "Circular construction/DfDisAssembly", component data and material passports making recovery and reuse economically viable, carried by 5 of the 50 cases [1], and VA15 enablesCapability VA4 "Material/energy saving/reduce CO2/waste", reversible connection design enabling material recovery where glued and monolithic joints limit salvage, carried by 6 of the 50 cases [1].

**The deployed record**

Several deployed processes show the off-site timber pattern at full maturity. census_RXH10-2 performs assembly and timber joinery cutting, works on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, and is at technology readiness level 9 [2], and it uses timber [3]; the context names no firm behind it. RP6 performs assembly and timber joinery cutting on the structural core, deployed off-site, at technology readiness level 9 [4], and RP7 does the same work off-site, adopted to address digital and market drivers, also at technology readiness level 9 [5]. On the facade specifically, RP8 performs inspection and material handling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, deployed off-site, at technology readiness level 9 [6], and RP17 performs inspection on the facade on site, outdoors, at technology readiness level 9 [7]. Two further timber records carry a named developer but no process profile: census_RXT1-2, developed by Firm_128, in timber [8], and census_RXT9-1, developed by Firm_171, in timber [9].

Two limits on that evidence. The context does not link any of these cases to the enablers above, so I cannot say which of them exhibits prefabrication, a configurator or early contractor involvement; the activation counts quoted are for the coded record as a whole. And the material and process lists retrieved here are a selection, not a complete inventory, so the absence of a given timber facade case from them is not evidence that none exists.
